1 Introduction
This document accompanies the external review of the following datasets:
• spodumene concentrate production | AU
• lithium brine concentration | CN
• lithium carbonate production, battery grade, from concentrated brine | CN
• lithium brine concentration | US
• lithium carbonate production, battery grade, from concentrated brine | US
• lithium brine concentration, Fenix | AR
• lithium carbonate production, battery grade, from concentrated brine, Fenix | AR
• lithium brine concentration, Salar de Olaroz | AR
• lithium carbonate production, battery grade, from concentrated brine, Salar de Olaroz |
AR
Additionally, it provides an overview of the current ecoinvent framework for lithium in order to
give historical context, and presents the new framework and the regions that will be covered.
The document focuses on the datasets submitted to ecoinvent and supports the reviewer in
understanding dataset scope, methodological choices, and consistency with the framework.
Datasets that are part of the BRGM submission will be documented in a separate report that
details modelling decisions, assumptions, data sources, and any related methodological
choices.
The report provides:
• Context and system boundaries for the datasets
• Key modelling decisions and deviations from original sources
• Mass balance information
• Climate change scores and comparison with literature
3

2 Background
2.1 Current Lithium production dataset (upstream)
The goal of this data submission is to improve the lithium supply chain in ecoinvent. The current
structure of the lithium supply chain is shown below. Lithium hydroxide is then produced from
lithium carbonate GLO.
Figure 1: ecoinvent v3.12 lithium framework
Here the list of the datasets currently available in ecoinvent, with link to ecoQuery:
- Lithium brine inspissation | GLO
- Market for lithium brine, 6.7% Li | GLO
- Lithium carbonate production, from concentrated brine | GLO
- Spodumene production | AU

4

3 New framework
To address the gaps and improve geographical specificity in ecoinvent's lithium supply chain,
we have developed a comprehensive framework that captures the diversity of lithium
production pathways globally, with recent data from literature. This framework distinguishes
between two primary lithium extraction routes, hard-rock mining (spodumene) and brine
extraction, and models region-specific processing chains that reflect current production
methods and geographical representation.
The framework captures the complete supply chain for lithium carbonate production from both
primary extraction routes. For brine-based sources, this includes evaporation pond operations
to concentrate lithium-bearing brines, followed by chemical conversion to produce battery-
grade lithium carbonate (Li₂CO₃). For hard-rock sources, the chain covers mining operations
and beneficiation to produce spodumene concentrate in Australia, and subsequent chemical
conversion in China to produce battery-grade lithium carbonate from the imported Australian
spodumene.
Additionally, lithium hydroxide monohydrate (LiOH·H₂O) production is also covered in China
and Chile.
The framework thus captures the complete upstream-to-midstream supply chain, enabling
comprehensive life cycle assessments from raw material extraction through to the two main
lithium chemical products used in battery manufacturing.
This structured approach enables more accurate life cycle assessments by:
- Providing geographically differentiated datasets for key production regions (Australia,
China, United States, and Argentina)
- Distinguishing between different salar operations where multiple sites exist within the
same country
- Ensuring methodological consistency across all datasets
Figure 2 and Table 1 below show the complete structure of activities and reference products.
Please note that the new framework will fully replace all the existing datasets in ecoinvent
v3.12 and prior. Only the dataset ‘lithium hydroxide production’ will stay in the next release, as
this dataset represents the anhydrous technical grade of lithium hydroxide, typically used in the
production of products such as: adhesives and sealants, lubricants and greases, fillers,
putties, plasters, modelling clay, hydraulic fluids and metal working fluids.

5 ecoinvent submission
5.1 Spodumene production
The primary reference for this dataset is:
Khakmardan, S., Crawford, R. H., Giurco, D., & Li, W. (2025). Constructing a life cycle inventory
of Spodumene concentrate production: Greenbushes case, Western Australia. Journal of
Cleaner Production, 496, 145123. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jclepro.2025.145123
This dataset represents the cradle-to-gate life cycle inventory for spodumene concentrate
(SC6, ~6% Li₂O) produced at the Greenbushes operation in Western Australia for the year 2022.
System Boundaries and Scope
The dataset covers the complete production chain from ore extraction to the processing plant
gate, with spodumene concentrate as the reference product. The system boundaries include:
• Mining operations: Open-pit mining with conventional drilling and blasting, overburden
removal and waste handling, ore loading and on-site haulage, and all auxiliary mine
operations including mine infrastructure and land use
• Beneficiation and processing: Crushing and screening, dense media separation using
ferrosilicon, grinding and classification, flotation using fatty acid collector and glycol-
based frother with pH modifiers, filtration and dewatering, and tailings management.
The functional unit is 1 kg of dewatered spodumene concentrate containing approximately 6%
Li₂O. The dataset excludes downstream transport and chemical conversion processes.
Modelling choices in ecoinvent:
1. The original paper excludes the tantalum byproduct from LCIA due to its negligible mass
ratio relative to SC6. In ecoinvent, economic allocation is applied for the tantalum
concentrate co-product (30% Ta₂O₅); however, given the minimal mass contribution,
the allocation factor remains negligible and results are comparable.
2. Compared to the paper, three specific exchanges were approximated due to the
unavailability of detailed equipment-specific data in the ecoinvent database and
unavailability of enough data to recreate their inventories:
o “blasthole drilling by D65”, proxied with an addition of diesel for blasthole drilling
(111MJ*0.000325 m = 0.036075MJ)
o “excavation by CAT 6015 excavator” proxied with “excavation, hydraulic digger”
o “haul by CAT 777 mining truck”, proxied with “transport, freight, lorry, >32 metric
ton, diesel, EUR 4”
9

These three exchanges collectively would contribute approximately 6% (0.02 kg CO₂eq/kg
spodumene concentrate) to the global warming potential. It is recommended to improve the
representation of these exchanges in future database updates and this is flagged in the
IncludedActivityEnd field of the dataset.
Exchange flow for road use:
“mining road” and “mining road maintenance” were created by the authors based on ecoinvent
“road” and “road maintenance”. We have introduced them with the original ecoinvent names.
Mass balance
The mass balance for this dataset can be found in the Excel unit process balance (spodumene,
undef).xlsx.
In the Excel document, it is possible to observe for each property whether there is a balance
between the input and output, and which exchanges mostly contribute to it.
Ideally, it is advisable to allow a maximum of 1% difference between input and output for each
property, with 5% as a worst-case scenario. Therefore, it is required to carefully review the
properties where this limit is trespassed. Please note that wet mass = dry mass + water in wet
mass
Mass balance key highlights:
• Wet mass shows an imbalance of 0.43%, which we consider acceptable
• Dry mass and water content in wet mass show an imbalance of 7.23% and 35.37%,
respectively. These imbalances were investigated: the imbalance is driven by the
default ecoinvent properties automatically assigned to the exchange “non sulfidic
tailing, off-site” (30% water). The paper does not report a specific tailings
composition/water content. If the tailings were assumed to be dry, the balances would
close.
• Lithium content in spodumene from ground: Lithium is imbalanced because the Li
content is based on default ecoinvent properties for “spodumene from ground”. Action
point: We suggest balancing the lithium output via the properties of ‘spodumene from
ground’ to maintain elemental closure.
• Other elements (Al, Si. O): we observe an imbalance because these elments are
present in ecoinvent’s default “spodumene from ground” properties but not reported
for the concentrate output. Action point: we propose either updating output
‘spodumene concentrate’ properties or adding a note in the metadata.
10

5.2 Lithium brine concentration and lithium carbonate,
battery grade production
This section presents the lithium brine concentration and lithium carbonate production
datasets for multiple salars. While site-specific details and considerations are discussed
individually for each salar, several methodological choices and data treatment approaches are
common across all brine-based datasets. These shared elements are described below before
presenting the individual salars’ datasets.
Data Source
The lithium brine concentration and lithium carbonate production datasets presented here are
based on the modeling work of Schenker & Pfister (2025), which represents an updated and
expanded version of earlier 2022 framework:
• Schenker, V., & Pfister, S. (2025). Current and Future Impacts of Lithium Carbonate
from Brines: A Global Regionalized Life Cycle Assessment Model. Environmental
Science & Technology, 59(13), 6543-6555.
This 2025 publication builds upon and updates the methodology presented in:
• Schenker, V., Oberschelp, C., & Pfister, S. (2022). Regionalized life cycle assessment of
present and future lithium production for Li-ion batteries. Resources, Conservation and
Recycling, 187, 106611.
Scaling Methodology: Evaporation Ponds to Concentrated Brine
Schenker & Pfister (2025) model the evaporation pond process as producing one functional unit
per "unit of evaporation pond" or “unit of DLE evaporation ponds”, according to the site
operation mode. To integrate these inventories into ecoinvent framework, we needed to scale
the evaporation pond inventories to the reference product "concentrated lithium brine, x% Li"
(expressed per kg of concentrated brine).
This scaling is essential because the concentrated brine is the intermediate product that
feeds into lithium carbonate production.
The scaling approach uses the lithium mass balance between raw brine input and concentrated
brine output, along with site-specific lithium concentrations. Using Salar de Olaroz as an
example, with the data from Schenker & Pfister:
• 1 unit of evaporation pond requires 0.02446 kg of lithium from the environment (raw
brine input)
• 1 kg of lithium carbonate battery grade requires 0.348 kg of lithium from the
environment (computing from the cradle-to-gate data reported in Schenker)
• Therefore, 1 kg of lithium carbonate battery grade requires 14.25 units of evaporation
pond (calculated as 0.348 kg of Li per kg Li2CO3/ 0.02446 kg of Li per unit)
12

• The raw lithium brine has a lithium concentration of 0.06% Li by weight according to
Schenker & Pfister (2025), Sheet 'B.2_LCI - Input data'
• The concentrated lithium brine has a lithium concentration of 1.20% Li by weight
according to Schenker & Pfister (2025), Sheet 'B.2_LCI - Input data'
To calculate the concentrated brine produced per evaporation pond unit:
• 29 kg of concentrated brine per kg of lithium carbonate are required (calculated as
0.348 kg of Li per kg Li2CO3 / 0.012 kg Li per kg conc. Li brine)
• 2.04 kg of concentrated brine per pond unit are produced (calculated as 29 kg / 14.25
units of evaporation)
Result: 2.04 kg of concentrated lithium brine (1.2% Li) are produced per 1 unit of evaporation
pond at Salar de Olaroz. Therefore, if we use the reference product "lithium brine,
concentrated, 1.2% Li", we need to divide the amount of each exchange in the inventory of
Schenker and Pfister for the evaporation pond by a factor of 2.04 to express it per kg of
concentrated brine.
This scaling methodology was applied consistently across all datasets to ensure that
evaporation pond inventories from Schenker & Pfister (2025) are correctly expressed per
kg of concentrated brine, enabling proper integration with downstream lithium carbonate
production processes.
Exchanges comments
We plan to improve the exchanges comments inside the ecoinvent datasets.
We had originally structured them to mention from which process step in the model of
Schenker the amounts are taken from. However, we are now reconsidering this approach as we
think that only mentioning the process step of the model might not be the most straightforward
way for users to grasp the role of each exchange. We plan to work on exchange comments
improvement during the first review round, we will then resubmit the datasets with these
updates during the second review round together with the addressing of the comments
from the reviewer. We report here 2 examples of how we plan to work on the comments, from
the dataset ‘lithium brine concentration, Salar de Olaroz | AR’:
1. Current comment to the exchange ‘sulfuric acid’: From Schenker & Pfister,
2025. SI. Used in the process Water_Ola, df_evaporation_ponds. Scaled to 1 kg
of concentrated lithium brine (2.04kg of concentrated lithium brine per kg of
evaporation pond)
To implement comment to the exchange ‘sulfuric acid’: Sulfuric acid is used for
pH adjustment during brine processing in evaporation ponds to optimize lithium
precipitation and minimize magnesium co-precipitation. From Schenker &
Pfister, 2025. SI. Allocated to the process df_evaporation_ponds. Scaled to 1 kg
of concentrated lithium brine (2.04 kg of concentrated lithium brine per kg of
evaporation pond output).
2. Current comment to the exchange ‘quicklime, milled, packed’: From Schenker &
Pfister, 2025. SI. Used in the process df_evaporation_ponds. Scaled to 1 kg of
concentrated lithium brine (2.04kg of concentrated lithium brine per kg of
13

pages.text:
evaporation pond)
To implement comment to the exchange ‘quicklime, milled, packed’ ‘:
Quicklime (CaO) is used in the brine concentration stage (evaporation pond
system / associated brine treatment) to precipitate and remove dissolved
impurities (e.g. Mg) from the brine prior to downstream processing. Amount
based on Schenker & Pfister (2025) Supplementary Information, where it is
modelled as an input to df_evaporation_ponds. Scaled for this dataset to 1 kg
concentrated lithium brine, using the factor 2.04 kg concentrated brine per 1 kg
evaporation pond output.
Soda ash
This section addresses a general specification issue regarding soda ash.
A discrepancy exists across literature sources regarding whether "soda ash, light" or "soda ash,
dense" is used. Schenker & Pfister (2025) explicitly uses "soda ash, light". Kelly et al. (2021)
report "soda ash" generically (Table S.6 and S.7, Supplementary Information) without specifying
light or dense, but Chordia et al. (2022) explicitly map this to "soda ash, dense".
A soda ash study from the Argentinian government indicates that natural soda ash is
predominantly used for large-volume industrial applications, such as chemical precipitation
and mineral processing, and is associated with lower energy use and CO₂ emissions than
synthetic soda ash; however, as ecoinvent does not currently provide an explicit dataset for
natural soda ash, the background system necessarily relies on synthetic soda ash.
All ecoinvent datasets currently use "soda ash, dense". Action point We seek the reviewer's
advice on the most appropriate choice between "soda ash, light” and "soda ash, dense’’. This
specification has a substantial impact on the IPCC 2021 GWP100 scores (climate change:
total, excl. biogenic CO₂), as the two soda ash types have significantly different emission
factors in ecoinvent. The influence of this choice on the carbon footprint can be observed in the
GWP100 scores presented in the following sections.
Please note that also for the spodumene dataset the exchange ‘soda ash, dense’ was selected,
as also Khakmardan does not specify further the type of soda ash. The effect in spodumene is
smaller, as reported in the Scores section of the spodumene dataset.
14

5.2.1 Sites overview
This section presents an overview of the sites covered together with estimation of the GWP100
score of each dataset. Please keep in mind that these are estimations based on v3.12
framework and that the final scores will be affected by next iterations in this project and
updates in other areas of the database.
5.2.1.1 Chaerhan,CN
Process Overview and Dataset Boundaries
The Chaerhan lithium production route follows a DLE-based process sequence as illustrated
below from Schenker & Pfister (2025). The complete production chain includes:
1. Evaporation ponds/pumping
2. Li-ion selective adsorption (DLE)
3. Ion exchanger (low water)
4. Nanofiltration
5. Reverse osmosis
6. DLE evaporation ponds
7. Li₂CO₃ precipitation (TG)
8. Centrifuge Li₂CO₃ (TG) / Washing Li₂CO₃ (TG)
9. Dissolution
10. Li₂CO₃ precipitation (BG)
11. Centrifuge Li₂CO₃ (BG) / Washing Li₂CO₃ (BG)
12. Centrifuge washing
13. Rotary dryer
Dataset boundary definition:
• ecoinvent lithium brine concentration dataset (CN) covers steps 1-6 in the process
sequence (evaporation ponds/pumping through DLE evaporation ponds), producing
concentrated lithium brine at 0.022% Li as the reference product. This represents the
upstream brine enrichment and concentration processes.
• ecoinvent lithium carbonate production dataset (CN) begins at step 7 and covers
all downstream processing (Li₂CO₃ precipitation through rotary dryer), using the
15

concentrated brine (0.022% Li) as input and producing battery-grade Li₂CO₃ as the
reference product.
Geography: Chaerhan (Qarhan) salt lake, Qinghai Province, China. Feed brine is reported
as brine/pulp from a K-fertilizer plant, with Li concentration 0.25–0.6 g/L.<
Time period: Current operation representative for the early-2020s
Technology:
• DLE-type brine concentration route using Li-ion selective adsorption with adsorption
and desorption phases (with heating), followed by downstream volume-
reduction/purification through ion exchange and membrane filtration (nanofiltration +
reverse osmosis). In the Schenker & Pfister 2025 framework, Chaerhan is highlighted
as a special DLE case relying mainly on volume reduction and not reporting a
separate pretreatment phase before the DLE column (unlike other DLE sites).
Output: Concentrated lithium brine, 0.022% Li
• Battery-grade production is modeled with the brine-to-Li₂CO₃ processing structure
shown above from Schenker & Pfister (2025). CO₂ is largely recycled within the
upgrading loop as described in the Schenker & Pfister (2025) model documentation.
Energy and material calculations follow the Schenker & Pfister (2025) Supplementary
Information process modules.
Output: Battery-grade Li₂CO₃
GWP100 Score (IPCC 2021)
No score estimation for the brine is reported in Schenker & Pfister 2025.

5.2.1.2 Salar de Olaroz, AR
Process Overview and Dataset Boundaries
The Salar de Olaroz lithium production route follows a conventional evaporation pond
concentration followed by intensive purification and upgrading sequence, as illustrated in in
the flowchart below from Schenker & Pfister (2025). The complete production chain includes:
1. Evaporation ponds/pumping
2. Centrifuge (general)
3. Li₂CO₃ precipitation (TG)
4. Washing Li₂CO₃ (TG)
5. Centrifuge Li₂CO₃ (TG)
6. Dissolution
7. Centrifuge (general)
8. Ion exchanger (high water) - First purification stage
9. Ion exchanger (high water) - Ca/Mg removal
10. Ion exchanger (low water) - boron removal
11. Li₂CO₃ precipitation (BG)
12. Centrifuge Li₂CO₃ (BG)
13. Washing Li₂CO₃ (BG)
14. Centrifuge washing
15. Rotary dryer
Dataset boundary definition:
• ecoinvent lithium brine concentration, Salar de Olaroz dataset (AR) covers step 1
in the process sequence (evaporation ponds/pumping with quicklime addition for
Mg/Ca removal), producing concentrated lithium brine at 1.2% Li as the reference
product. The process includes volume reduction in evaporation ponds and
acidification using sulfuric acid for pH adjustment.
• ecoinvent lithium carbonate production, battery grade, from concentrated brine,
Salar de Olaroz dataset (AR) begins at step 2 and covers all downstream
processing (Li₂CO₃ precipitation through rotary dryer), using the concentrated brine
(1.2% Li) as input and producing battery-grade Li₂CO₃ as the reference product. This
stage includes the intensive ion exchanger treatment (steps 8-10) that characterizes
Olaroz operations.
18

Geography: Salar de Olaroz, Argentina
Time period: Dataset represents operations from 2011-2019, with time validity set to 2019
to reflect the key operational reporting year used for Olaroz assumptions.
Technology:
• Conventional salar concentration via evaporation ponds. Brine is pumped from 50 m
below ground and concentrated by solar evaporation to ~1.2 wt% Li. The process
includes volume reduction in evaporation ponds with quicklime addition for
magnesium and calcium removal, followed by acidification using sulfuric acid for pH
adjustment and centrifugation for solid-liquid separation.
Output: Concentrated lithium brine, 1.2% Li
• Conventional brine-route upgrading to battery grade via two-stage
precipitation/upgrading. Technical-grade Li₂CO₃ is precipitated with soda ash
(modeled stoichiometrically with surplus to account for losses in Schenker & Pfister),
followed by washing and centrifugation. The technical-grade Li₂CO₃ is then dissolved
at low temperature with CO₂ to improve dissolution. Before battery-grade
precipitation, the solution undergoes intensive purification through ion exchangers.
The intensive purification through three ion exchangers during the carbonate
production stage is an Olaroz-specific process characteristic: two for Ca/Mg removal
(high water) and one for boron removal (low water).
Battery-grade Li₂CO₃ is then precipitated with CO₂ recirculation, followed by
centrifugation, washing, and drying (rotary dryer).
Output: Battery-grade Li₂CO₃
Complementary information:
From direct communication with the authors, we know that the model for Olaroz is very
likely underestimating salt tailings (which are reported at 9.9e-17 kg of salt tailings at the
evaporation pond). This is due to lack of reported enriched brine chemistry in the
evaporation ponds at the site. As a result, the reported values for salt tailings in the
publication are too and should not be considered confirmed. ecoinvent dataset does not
include salt tailings.
19

GWP100 Score (IPCC 2021)
No score estimation for the brine is reported in Schenker & Pfister 2025.

complete production chain includes:
1. Evaporation ponds/pumping
2. Mg and Ca removal by soda ash
3. Acidification
4. Li-ion selective adsorption (DLE)
5. Mechanical evaporator
6. Ion exchanger (low water)
7. DLE evaporation ponds

9. Centrifuge Li₂CO₃ (TG)

11. Dissolution

13. Centrifuge Li₂CO₃ (BG)
14. Washing Li₂CO₃ (BG)

Dataset boundary definition:

5.2.2 Mass balance in lithium brine concentration datasets
A document in support of the mass balance analysis has been shared with this report unit
process balance (brine concentration, undef).xlsx.
In the Excel document, it is possible to observe for each property whether there is a balance
between the input and output, and which exchanges mostly contribute to it.
The Excel shows 1 sheet for each site.
An important methodological consideration affects the interpretation of these mass balances.
The source literature (Schenker & Pfister, 2025) follows the AWARE methodology for water
scarcity assessment, as recommended by the UNEP-SETAC Life Cycle Initiative. This
methodology specifically excludes saline brine water from water consumption accounting,
focusing only on freshwater consumption.
As stated in Schenker & Pfister (2025, p. E): "Kelly et al., Chordia et al., and Schenker et al.
do not include the water content of the brine in their assessments when assessing water
scarcity. As AWARE is designed to only assess freshwater consumption, we follow the
approach defined by the UNEP-SETAC Life Cycle Initiative."
A complete mass balance for lithium brine concentration should account for:
26

Inputs:
• Raw lithium brine (with specified water content and dissolved mineral composition)
• Freshwater (for washing, dust suppression, or dilution)
• Process chemicals (acids, bases, flocculants as applicable)
Outputs:
• Concentrated lithium brine (with specified water content and mineral composition)
• Evaporated water
• Precipitated salt tailings (primarily NaCl, but also K, Mg, Ca, and sulfate salts)
Current data gaps affecting mass balance
Beyond the exclusion of brine water from water consumption accounting, additional data
gaps contribute to the incomplete mass balance in these datasets:
Missing mineral extraction flows: Because the brine water itself is not reported as an input
flow (consistent with AWARE), the dissolved minerals carried in that brine water are also not
explicitly reported as extractions from ground.
Incomplete salt tailings reporting: As communicated by the dataset authors, salt tailings
data is incomplete or missing in the current datasets.
Planned actions on the ecoinvent side
To address the identified mass balance issues while respecting the methodological choices
in the source literature, we plan to implement the following improvements:
1. Include lithium brine composition in the reference product
At the moment, we included in the Reference Product properties only the lithium content.
We will incorporate the brine composition data (water content and dissolved mineral
concentrations) as properties of the concentrated lithium brine reference product, based on
the data available in Schenker & Pfister (2025), Sheet 'B.2_LCI - Input data'.
This will provide users with transparent information about the actual composition of the
output brine. In particular, the water content will be accounted for.
Action point: Brine composition data is not available for all sites in the Schenker dataset.
For sites where composition data is missing (Olaroz, Silver Peak and Fenix), we seek editor
advice on selecting an appropriate proxy for brine composition when missing. The
sheet 'B.2_LCI - Input data' has been reported in the attached Excel unit process balance
(brine concentration, undef).xlsx.
2. Document methodology and data gaps
We propose to clearly document in the dataset metadata:
• The application of the AWARE methodology for water accounting, which deliberately
excludes saline brine water from water consumption metrics
• The current data gaps regarding precipitated salts and complete water balance
27

This transparent documentation will help LCA practitioners understand the limitations of
these datasets.
3. Parallel improvements for current or future releases
In parallel with the above actions, we will continue working on the following aspects, either
during this release or in subsequent updates:
• New biosphere flows: Consider introducing a new elementary flow such as "water,
brine, from ground" to distinguish ancient saline brine water from freshwater
extraction, allowing for complete water accounting while maintaining compatibility
with AWARE methodology
• Salt tailings data: Work to fill the data gaps on precipitated salts, potentially by
reaching out to the dataset authors (Schenker & Pfister) for clarification on additional
calculations or proxy data
• Complete mineral balance: Develop a more comprehensive approach to tracking all
dissolved minerals extracted with the brine and their fate during the concentration
process
These parallel improvements would enhance the datasets' utility for a broader range of LCA
applications while maintaining their validity for water scarcity assessment under AWARE
guidelines.
